transcript:
Meeting header: 
Date: 2027-11-29 14:00 UTC | Duration: ~49m | Recording: yes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramirez (Redwood SE), Anika Bose (Redwood SE), Priya Kapoor (Auriga Head of Platform), Liam O'Neal (CTO), Samir Bhattacharya (SecOps), Elena Park (ML Eng), Tom Reeves (SRE)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be rough): Auriga is evaluating Redwood Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private. Primary drivers: consistent 95th pct gen latency < 200ms for interactive chat, isolation for regulated customer data, and ability to handle irregular burst spikes (10-15x daily). They have an internal infra team but want to offload inference ops. Next: send pricing, run benchmark window with representative traces, follow-up deep dive on KMS/HSM for Private.

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya, AE on the Redwood side, and we have Diego and Anika with me. Quick round robin?
[00:12] Priya Kapoor: Hi, Priya here. Head of Platform at Auriga.
[00:15] Liam O'Neal: Liam, CTO.
[00:18] Samir Bhattacharya: Samir, security.
[00:20] Elena Park: Elena, ML.
[00:22] Tom Reeves: Tom, SRE.
[00:24] Diego Ramirez: Awesome, thanks. We'll keep this high level and then dig into sizing and burst patterns.

[01:05] Maya Chen: Quick context: from our intake form you mentioned two main workloads: an interactive chat assistant used by customers and a nightly summarization batch. Chat is latency-sensitive, summarization is throughputy but can be batched. Correct?
[01:18] Priya: Yep. Chat is the real stickiness — we need snappy responses. We instrumented p99 but want 95th at or below 200 millis for… for typical prompts. Not strict p99 SLA but 95th we care about. Summaries can take longer.
[01:40] Liam: We also have regulatory customers who require tenant isolation and strict audit logs. That pushes us to either dedicated pools or Private.

[02:10] Anika Bose: When you say tenant isolation, do you mean per-customer dedicated nodes or logical isolation within a shared pool?
[02:20] Samir: For us it's a mix. High-risk customers get dedicated pools — full node reservation. Mid-tier customers are fine with logical tenancy but with strong RBAC and audit trails.

[03:05] Diego: That's helpful. On the reserved capacity side we typically ask for a traffic profile — RPS by hour, typical token length, concurrency distribution. Can you share 72 hours of traffic traces and some example prompts?
[03:20] Elena: Yes, we can. We'll anonymize them but keep distribution. We'll also include a couple of adversarial prompts for rate tests.

[04:10] Tom: One question — what does your warm-pool / prewarm look like? We see large spikes when product releases hit and we need 10-15x bursts for 20 to 40 minutes.
[04:22] Diego: Good question. We support prewarmed hot pools and we also recommend a hybrid approach: a minimum reserved hot-set with autoscaleable warm nodes. The warm nodes can be pre-quantized or use faster kernels to reduce per-token cost.
[04:40] Maya: We usually model two levers: reserved baseline (for steady load) and burst headroom (for expected spikes). For example, customers keep 20-30% of peak as reserved and allow for burst up to 10x with overflow routing to cheaper variants or lower-weight models.

[05:15] Priya: Cheaper variants — do you mean smaller models or quantized versions?
[05:20] Anika: Both. We can route to a distilled or int8-quantized variant during capacity pressure. There's also option to have a fallback throughput tier with slightly higher latency but guaranteed throughput.

[06:02] Samir: Security — we need to validate encryption in transit and at rest, and KMS integration. If we go Private, HSM-backed keys are required. Can you confirm Redwood Private supports HSM?
[06:18] Diego: Short answer: yes. The Private deployment supports customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations. We do have an audit trail for key usage and can provide architecture docs. We'll follow up with specifics.

[07:00] Liam: How do you handle KV cache isolation? We want to avoid cross-tenant KV cache leakage.
[07:12] Diego: KV cache is per-session and can be tenant-scoped. For Dedicated we can pin cache to tenant-specific processes or isolated CUDA contexts. For Private/on-prem we can fully isolate at the process and node level.
[07:35] Elena: Sometimes transcripts show mismatched tokens in transcripts — we've seen misattributions in other products — is there a way to tag logs to tenant ids?
[07:45] Anika: Yes, token-level tracing can include tenant id hash, request id, and prompt fingerprint. We can provide an example log format.

[08:30] Tom: Latency — we need worst-case tail behavior: do you do continuous batching? How does batching affect 95th?
[08:42] Diego: We use workload-aware batching with latency SLOs enforced at the router. For interactive flows we keep batch sizes small and favor 95th latency; for background tasks we batch larger to optimize throughput. The runtime will drop into lower-cost kernels for larger batches.

[09:20] Priya: Cost — what's the rough delta between Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private? Ballpark numbers are fine.
[09:30] Maya: Hosted is typically pay-as-you-go with higher unit cost but no infra ops. Dedicated gives predictable monthly commit with lower unit price; Private has platform licensing plus infra and support. We'll send a dedicated pricing spreadsheet, but ballpark: Dedicated can be 30-50% cheaper per-token at scale versus hosted, depending on utilization.

[10:15] Liam: Preemption — if we reserve nodes, are they preemptible? We can't have preemptions for certain tenants.
[10:24] Diego: Reserved pools are non-preemptible for the committed capacity. We do offer burstable capacity using spot or lower-tier nodes that could be preempted; customers route non-critical traffic there.

[11:05] Priya: For our regulated customers we need SOC 2 + ISO reports and an exportable audit log for each request.
[11:12] Maya: We have SOC2 and ISO artifacts; we'll attach them. Audit logs are exportable with tenant-scoped filters.

[12:00] Tom: In the event of a large sudden spike, can Redwood spin up GPU capacity in under 5 minutes or do you recommend warm pools?
[12:12] Diego: Cold spin-up to fully provisioned GPUs can take longer depending on cloud region; we recommend maintaining a warm-pool to meet sub-5 minute ramp. The warm-pool is typically preloaded with model weights and warmed kv cache to shave minutes into seconds.

[13:00] Elena: What's the overhead of keeping a hot-pool (cost)? We need to justify baseline.
[13:10] Maya: Hot-pool cost depends on chosen GPU type and utilization. Often customers size hot-pool to cover 30-40% of peak for a good balance. Our Optimize team can run a cost-model: given traces we'll recommend amount to reserve vs burst.

[14:05] Samir: Compliance question: does Redwood support customer-managed audit retention windows and SSO/SAML for access to the Console?
[14:15] Anika: Yes. SSO/SAML, SCIM for provisioning, and configurable audit retention windows are supported on Dedicated and Private.

[15:02] Liam: We're curious about fallback behaviors — if a model variant is unavailable, what's the automatic policy?
[15:10] Diego: We support routing policies: fail open to lower-cost variants, queue with retry, or return a degraded response. You can configure per-route fallbacks and canary rollouts.

[15:45] Priya: For the benchmark, we want Redwood to replicate our production-ish traffic for 2 hours and show 95th percentile latency. Can you run that?
[15:53] Maya: Yes. We'll schedule a 30-60 minute benchmark window initially. For a full replication we recommend a 2-hour run during off-peak to reduce noise. Please share traces and we'll propose a plan.

[16:30] Tom: A technical nit — when you say quantized variants, does Redwood support int8 and int4 inference kernels on the same runtime?
[16:38] Diego: We support multiple quantization profiles and select kernels at runtime. For int4 we do have some model compatibility restrictions; we'll surface which models we can run int4 versus int8.

[17:05] Elena: Any limits on sequence length for warm-pool memory residency? Our prompts sometimes reach 3k tokens.
[17:12] Diego: We size KV cache and memory based on max context. For long-context workloads we'd recommend dedicated nodes with larger GPU memory or model offloading. We'll look at your 3k-token pattern in the traces.

[18:10] Priya: One operational concern: who owns alerting and runbooks during a dedicated incident?
[18:18] Maya: For Redwood-hosted Dedicated, alerting integrates with your PagerDuty; Redwood handles infra-level incidents per SLA, but we collaborate on runbooks. For Private, the customer owns infra runbooks, Redwood provides support escalation and playbooks.

[19:05] Liam: Can Dedicated be deployed within our VPC? We need IP allowlisting and peering for Private data flows.
[19:14] Anika: Dedicated can be configured with a private networking setup and peering to your VPC in many regions; Private is the more isolated option where everything runs in your VPC or on-prem.

[20:00] Samir: Encryption at rest — if we use Dedicated, will Redwood manage keys or can we bring keys?
[20:08] Diego: You can bring-your-own-keys (BYOK) for Dedicated in many setups; Private fully supports BYOK/HSM. We'll confirm exact options for your cloud region.

[21:00] Priya: We have an internal inference team curious about migration: is there a path to start Hosted, move to Dedicated, then Private?
[21:10] Maya: Absolutely. That's a common path. You get predictable performance, then commit to Dedicated as traffic grows, and if compliance requires it you go Private. The API and model versions remain consistent across modes.

[22:20] Elena: On telemetry — we want token-level cost breakdown per tenant and per-route latency percentiles. Can Redwood surface token-level cost?
[22:28] Anika: Yes, Console exposes token-level cost, per-route latency, and model-level breakdowns. We can also ship logs to your SIEM.

[23:10] Tom: Can we configure preemption windows on lower-priority tenants? Eg. if we need to reclaim burstable capacity.
[23:18] Diego: Yes, per-tenant priority and preemption windows are supported. You define which tenants are preemptible and which are protected.

[23:55] Priya: Any gotchas around autoscaling with reserved nodes? We don't want autoscaler to provision incompatible GPU types.
[24:05] Diego: We recommend configuring autoscaler constraints to preferred GPU families; the platform will respect node type affinities. We'll include recommended autoscaler configs.

[25:30] Maya: Let's talk numbers. Priya, do you have a target steady baseline and expected peak?
[25:38] Priya: Baseline is around 80 qps during business hours, peaks up to 1200 qps during product promos. Average token length is 80 tokens per request for chat.

[26:00] Diego: That 15x burst pattern definitely argues for hot pools plus overflow routing. We'll run a simulation against those traces.

[27:10] Liam: We also want to ensure that private data never leaves our VPC for certain customers. Is there an enclave or air-gapped option?
[27:20] Anika: For sensitive workloads we support Private on-prem deployments which are air-gapped. We can discuss offline the enrollment and support contract.

[28:05] Samir: Audit and legal would want to see contract language around data residency.
[28:12] Maya: We'll route that to our contracts team — include standard SLAs and addenda for data residency.

[29:00] Elena: About model rollouts — if we push a new model version and see quality regressions, can we automatically revert to previous variant?
[29:10] Diego: Yes, automated rollbacks and canary traffic are built-in: you can configure percent rollouts and automatic revert if key eval metrics drop.

[30:05] Priya: One more on cost control: can we preemptively route certain routes to lower-cost quantized variants at off-hours?
[30:14] Anika: Yes, routing policies can be schedule-based. You can set rules to switch model variants based on time, cost thresholds, or latency.

[31:00] Maya: Alright, quick recap of what we'll do next: we'll send the dedicated pricing sheet and warm-pool playbook; Diego will propose prewarm sizing after seeing traces; schedule benchmark window. Anything else?
[31:12] Priya: Please include compliance artifacts and KMS/HSM integration docs.
[31:20] Samir: And the audit log export format.

[32:00] Diego: Noted. We'll also include a sample autoscaler config and suggested node types for your region.

[33:30] Liam: Timeframe — we'd like to pilot in January. Is that realistic?
[33:38] Maya: Yes, assuming traces and initial benchmark go well, a January pilot is reasonable. We'll align on contract and sizing in December.

[34:15] Elena: Small thing — when you mention KV cache being per-session, please clarify TTL and eviction semantics. We had problems with stale caches in another product.
[34:25] Diego: TTLs are configurable per-route, and we expose eviction metrics. We'll include default suggestions (5-30 minutes) and per-route overrides.

[35:00] Priya: Any recommendations for model choice? We need a strong tradeoff between quality and latency.
[35:08] Anika: We typically recommend a medium-sized model for interactive chat with int8 quantization to hit 95th latency targets, and a larger model for batch summaries where throughput matters. We'll include model suggestions after reviewing your prompt set.

[36:10] Tom: Can Redwood integrate with our existing CI/CD to automate model rollouts?
[36:18] Diego: Yes, we have API hooks and a Git-backed model registry workflow; deployments can be triggered via CI and include policy checks.

[37:00] Maya: Any blockers or immediate concerns?
[37:05] Priya: Nothing blocking. Security wants the HSM proof, and platform wants traces.

[38:00] Maya: Great. We'll send the package within 48 hours.
[38:05] Elena: Thanks.
[38:10] Samir: Thanks, appreciate it.

[39:00] [wrap-up] Maya: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with docs and pencil in a benchmark slot for next week.
[39:10] Meeting ends.

Transcript notes: occasional transcription errors: "kay-vee cache" instead of KV cache; "S A M L" sometimes transcribed as "Sam L"; some overlaps not separated. Speakers are generally correct though a few lines attributed to "Speaker 2" in auto transcript were fixed in manual pass.
